questions.question: A raw JSON-RPC message has a method field but no id field at all. Which of the four MCP message shapes is it?
options: A request, because every message with a method field is a request
A result response, because the absence of an id means the exchange is already complete
An error response, because errors are the only shape that can omit an id
A notification, since only requests and results are required to carry an id
questions.explanation: A message with a method and no id field at all is a notification; JSON-RPC uses the presence of id to separate a request, which expects a reply, from a notification, which does not.

questions.question: A 2026-07-28 client receives a result object from a server implementing an earlier protocol version that never sends resultType. How must the client interpret the missing field?
options: As complete, the backward-compatible default for servers that predate resultType
As an error, since resultType is mandatory and its absence makes the result malformed
As whichever value the client used in its most recent request
As input_required, since missing information usually blocks completion
questions.explanation: For backward compatibility with servers implementing earlier protocol versions, a client must treat an absent resultType as complete rather than reject the response.

questions.question: Which _meta key prefix is reserved for MCP because its second dot-separated label is modelcontextprotocol or mcp?
options: com.example.mcp/, since mcp appears as its third label
dev.mcp/, since its second label is mcp
mcp.example/, since its first label is literally mcp
org.tools.mcp/, since mcp appears at the end of the prefix
questions.explanation: A prefix is reserved for MCP only when its second dot-separated label is modelcontextprotocol or mcp; dev.mcp qualifies because mcp sits in that second position, while the other prefixes place mcp elsewhere.

questions.question: A request's params._meta includes io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion but omits io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities entirely. What must a conformant server do?
options: Process the request as if the client declared no optional capabilities
Reject it with JSON-RPC error -32601, since the method itself is now unrecognized
Reject it with JSON-RPC error -32602, and 400 Bad Request on HTTP
Hold the request open until the client sends the missing field in a follow-up
questions.explanation: A request missing a required _meta field such as clientCapabilities is malformed, and a conformant server must reject it with -32602, returning 400 Bad Request on an HTTP transport.

questions.question: A gateway operator wants to route requests differently depending on which client sent them, reading io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo to decide. Why is that unsafe?
options: Only servers may read clientInfo; gateways are restricted to reading _meta.progressToken
The field never reaches the gateway because it is stripped before the request leaves the client
The field is only populated on the first request of a brand-new connection
clientInfo is self-reported by the sender and is never verified by the protocol
questions.explanation: clientInfo and serverInfo are self-reported by whoever sends them and are intended only for display, logging, and debugging, so a routing or authorization decision must never depend on them.

questions.question: A client has three independent requests ready to send to a Streamable HTTP server. What does 2026-07-28 require it to do?
options: Send three separate POST requests, one request or notification per body
Join them with newlines in one POST body, one message per line
Open a single SSE stream and push all three requests through it
Combine them into a single JSON-RPC batch array and POST it once
questions.explanation: JSON-RPC batching was removed from MCP in the 2025-06-18 revision, so each Streamable HTTP POST body must carry exactly one request or notification.
